text:
Can you guess the experiment? 🤔
Hint: this experiment sits 56 metres below ground. 

Here we see the journey from the #LHC tunnel all the way to the ALICE experiment detector, in its vast cavern, 56 metres below ground.

ALICE is CERN’s dedicated heavy-ion physics experiment, and just like the rest of the accelerator complex #AtCERN, it is currently undergoing major upgrade work.

These upgrades are in preparation for the #HiLumiLHC, which will dramatically improve the performance of the accelerator and bring an increased number of collisions.

Find out more about the ongoing upgrades at CERN: https://home.cern/science/long-shutdown-3/

text:
In the wake of partons 🌊

The CMS Experiment at CERN reports the first direct observation of a “wake” formed by a parton travelling through quark–gluon plasma.

By studying the quark–gluon plasma recreated by lead-nuclei collisions in the #LHC, the CMS Collaboration has directly observed how particles travelling through it leave a pattern similar to the wake left by a boat.

The image shows artist Larisa Barannikova’s impression of the wake left behind by a particle travelling through quark–gluon plasma.

🔗 Read more: https://home.cern/in-the-wake-of-partons/

text:
The beam stops here 🛑 

#ThrowbackThursday to September 1980 at the Super Proton Synchrotron (SPS), the second-largest machine in CERN’s accelerator complex.

Here we see the Target Beam Stopper Mobile (TBSM), a water-cooled beam dump designed to absorb the energy of the particles in a beam, which could move up and down.

This ability to move allowed the beam stopper to stay out of the beam line during normal operation and to protect the experts working in the accelerator tunnels.

#DidYouKnow: In 1983, running as a proton-antiproton collider, the SPS delivered the Nobel Prize winning discovery of the W and Z particles.

Find out more about the SPS: https://home.cern/science/accelerators/super-proton-synchrotron

text:
‘Tis the season of trick-or-treating… and #DarkMatter 🎃

#DidYouKnow that visible matter makes up only about 5% of the Universe? The rest is dark matter (27%) and dark energy (68%). Shining light on their mysteries is a key challenge for modern science.

Every year, #DarkMatterDay takes place as the same time as Halloween, so, to celebrate the two, CERN’s #PhotoOfTheWeek features Jack-o’-lanterns in front of the Globe of Science and Innovation.

The top pumpkin is carved with the ATLAS Experiment at CERN logo and the bottom one shows  an event display – a visual representation of data produced by a particle collision inside the ATLAS detector.

Find out more about #DarkMatter research at CERN: https://home.cern/science/physics/dark-matter/

text:
CERN-made #HiLumiLHC quadrupoles ready for installation 💫

The completion of these new quadrupole magnets – known as the inner triplet magnets – marks the culmination of more than three decades of research and development in niobium-tin (Nb₃Sn) superconducting magnet technology.

These magnets will provide the powerful focusing needed to squeeze the proton beams more tightly as they pass through the ATLAS Experiment at CERN and CMS Experiment at CERN. 

Read more: https://home.cern/cern-made-hilumi-lhc-quadrupoles-ready-for-installation/

text:
CERN’s first Innovation Hub pilot to open in Belgium 🇧🇪

CERN and POM Limburg, Limburg’s provincial development agency, signed an agreement today to establish the first CERN Innovation Hub pilot at Corda Campus in Hasselt, Belgium. 

The hub will give Belgian industry access to technologies and expertise developed #AtCERN.

Find out more: https://home.cern/cerns-first-innovation-hub-pilot-to-open-in-belgium/

text:
🚀 Ready to up your game in accelerator science?

The CERN Accelerator School (CAS), in collaboration with the European Spallation Source, is pleased to announce their residential course on Advanced Accelerator Physics.

Designed for physicists, engineers and researchers who want to get to grips with modern beam dynamics and machine technology, this is an intensive two week course combining deep theoretical understanding with practical training.

What to Expect:
📚Core Lectures: Advanced topics in non-linear dynamics, collective effects and instabilities, low emittance lattices, light sources, ERLs and advanced acceleration concepts

🙌 Hands-on tracks to gain practical experience: Radiofrequency Measurements & Simulations; Beam Instrumentation & Diagnostics; Beam Optics Design & Correction

📍 Helsingborg, Sweden
🗓️ 13 – 25 June 2027
🎓 Prerequisites: CAS Introductory course (or equivalent experience)
❗Registration closes 12th April 2027 

🔗 Apply now: https://cas.web.cern.ch/

text:
The journey of a magnet back to the surface 🧲

Here we see a 11.5 metres-long magnet weighing 23 tonnes, travelling underground, before being lifted 56 metres to the surface through the ALICE experiment.

Did you hear that CERN’s accelerator complex and experimental facilities are undergoing major maintenance and upgrade work?

This phase is expected to last up to four years and will involve thousands of experts across CERN’s sites and tunnels. The work will cover civil engineering, infrastructure consolidation, upgrades of facilities and the installation of cutting-edge technology.

Read more about the latest updates of the road to #HiLumiLHC: https://home.cern/science/long-shutdown-3/

text:
Can you guess what this is? 
Hint: it’s a piece that will soon belong to a 7000-tonne detector #AtCERN. 😉

Here we see the first ring of the ATLAS Experiment at CERN Inner Tracker (ITk) Pixel Inner System, loaded with detector modules by teams at SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory in early October.

ITk is a next-generation tracker that will transform the way the ATLAS experiment detects particle collisions for the #HiLumiLHC.

The ring will be located closer to the beam pipe than any other part of ATLAS, right at the heart of the detector, where protons collide in the #LHC.

The modules on the first side are now in place, and initial measurements confirm they are correctly positioned, providing an encouraging start to this stage of assembly.

Read more: https://home.cern/science/long-shutdown-3/ 

📸by  Philippe Grenier
